title: Irreducible polynomials with coefficient restrictions
subject: finite-fields
summary: Prescribed coefficients and allowed coefficient sets lead to different existence and counting problems. Trace and norm explain the first and constant coefficients; character sums and sieves treat more general restrictions.
questionsAnswered: Can any one coefficient of an irreducible polynomial be prescribed?
How many arbitrary coefficient positions can be prescribed?
What changes when every coefficient is restricted to a set?
How do the answers depend on the field size and the degree?

sections.title: The counting problem
sections.body:
Write \(f(x)=x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), with \(n\ge2\). The unrestricted number of monic irreducibles is \(N_q(n)\sim q^n/n\). We now restrict the coefficients before counting. If a coefficient is prescribed, its position matters; in particular, \(a_0=0\) forces a factor \(x\).

For a root \(\alpha\) of degree \(n\), the first coefficient is minus its trace and the constant coefficient is \((-1)^n\) times its norm. General coefficient prescriptions concern elementary symmetric functions of all Frobenius conjugates.

sections.title: Construction algorithms
sections.body:
A direct construction samples polynomials satisfying the chosen restrictions and applies the Frobenius irreducibility test. Every accepted polynomial is proved irreducible. An existence or counting theorem is needed to guarantee that the allowed set contains an irreducible polynomial, or to bound the expected number of trials.

If an extension field is already available, one can instead search for a degree-\(n\) element with the required symmetric functions of its conjugates, then form its minimal polynomial. Trace and norm conditions are especially natural in this formulation.

sections.title: One prescribed coefficient
sections.body:
Hansen–Mullen theorem

Let \(n\ge2\), \(0\le j

  • \(j=0\) and \(c=0\);
  • \(q\) is even and \((n,j,c)=(2,1,0)\).

The first exception forces a root at zero. In the second, \(x^2+a\) is a square in characteristic two, because every element of a finite field of characteristic two has a square root.

Wan proved the theorem when \(n\ge36\) or \(q>19\), and Ham and Mullen checked the remaining cases. Tuxanidy and Wang gave a later proof using periods of discrete Fourier transforms. The corresponding theorem for primitive polynomials has a different list of exceptions.

sections.title: Several prescribed coefficients
sections.body:
Let \(I\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) contain \(r\) prescribed positions, and choose the coefficients at those positions. Assume \(a_0\ne0\) if \(0\in I\). Pollack proves, for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), the uniform asymptotic formula \[\#\{f\text{ monic irreducible satisfying the prescriptions}\}\sim\sigma N_q(n),\qquad r\le(1-\varepsilon)\sqrt n,\] as \(n\to\infty\), where \[\sigma=\begin{cases}q^{-r},&0\notin I,\\q^{1-r}/(q-1),&0\in I.\end{cases}\] The uniformity includes the field, positions, and prescribed values. The second normalization reflects the nonzero constant coefficient of every degree-\(n\) irreducible.

Ha's results allow a positive proportion of positions. In particular, for every \(q\), if \(n\ge52\) and \(r\le n/10\), every such prescription occurs. For fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1/4\), \(n\ge8\), and \(q\ge q_0(\varepsilon)\), one may prescribe \(\lfloor(1/4-\varepsilon)n\rfloor\) coefficients. The proofs use exponential sums and a function-field form of the circle method.

Example

Over \(\mathbb F_2\), any six chosen coefficients of a monic polynomial of degree sixty may be prescribed, provided the constant coefficient is one if it is among them. Ha's theorem guarantees an irreducible polynomial satisfying those choices.

sections.title: Allowed sets of coefficients
sections.body:
Now let \(a_i\) range over an allowed set \(A_i\subseteq\mathbb F_q\), possibly different for each position. This is different from fixing a small number of coefficients. Porritt treats one common allowed set; Cheng allows the sets to vary with the position.

A consequence of Cheng's theorem is the following. Fix \(q\ge300\), and suppose \(A_i=\mathbb F_q\setminus R_i\) with \(|R_i|\le\sqrt q/2\). As \(n\to\infty\), \[\#\{f\text{ monic irreducible}:a_i\in A_i\}=\frac{q}{n(q-1)}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}|A_i|\left(\frac{|A_0\setminus\{0\}|}{|A_0|}+O(q^{-\sqrt{n/45}})\right).\] The paper gives an explicit lower bound on \(n\) for this estimate.

For instance, requiring every nonleading coefficient to be nonzero gives the main term \(q(q-1)^{n-1}/n\). The constant coefficient enters separately because a zero there always makes a polynomial of degree at least two reducible.

sections.title: Square coefficients
sections.body:
Fix \(n\ge1\). Choose the nonleading coefficients independently and uniformly from the set \(S_q=\{a^2:a\in\mathbb F_q\}\), including zero. Bary-Soroker and Shmueli prove \[\Pr(f\text{ is irreducible over }\mathbb F_q)=\frac1n+O_n(q^{-1/2})\qquad(q\to\infty).\] For odd \(q\), uniform sampling from \(S_q\) differs from squaring a uniform random element of \(\mathbb F_q\): in the latter model, zero has half the probability of each nonzero square. For even \(q\), \(S_q=\mathbb F_q\).

Example

The squares in \(\mathbb F_5\) are \(0,1,4\). The polynomial \(x^2+x+1\) has square coefficients and is irreducible because its discriminant is \(2\), a nonsquare. The polynomial \(x^2+1\) also has square coefficients, but it factors as \((x-2)(x+2)\).

This theorem fixes the degree and lets the field size grow. It does not assert the same estimate for fixed \(q\) as the degree grows. Its proof uses Galois groups of function-field extensions and finite-field point counting.

sections.title: Factorization types
sections.body: Counting irreducibles is one case of counting factorization types. A type records the degrees of the irreducible factors. For unrestricted polynomials, unique factorization gives exact counts; for suitable families over growing finite fields, the limiting proportions are those of permutation cycle types. See factorization statistics for the formulas and short-interval theorem.

sections.title: Primitive and normal roots
sections.body: Coefficient restrictions can be combined with conditions on a root. A primitive root generates \(\mathbb F_{q^n}^{\times}\); a normal root has conjugates forming a basis over \(\mathbb F_q\). These requirements are stronger than having degree \(n\). In particular, a normal root has nonzero trace, so its minimal polynomial cannot have a zero coefficient of \(x^{n-1}\). See primitive and normal elements for tests and existence theorems.

sections.title: Complete normality
sections.body: Complete normality requires normality over every intermediate field. The Morgan–Mullen conjecture asks whether it can always be combined with primitivity. Published ranges and Hellwig's 2026 claimed resolution are recorded in the account of complete normality.

questions.title: Can any one coefficient be prescribed?
questions.scope: Monic degree n≥2 polynomials over every finite field
questions.body: Yes, with exactly the constant-zero and even-characteristic quadratic exceptions stated above. Primitive-polynomial prescriptions are a different problem with additional multiplicative conditions.

questions.title: Which coefficient positions allow stronger bounds?
questions.scope: Fixed finite field, growing degree, and a specified family of prescription patterns
questions.body: For a specified pattern of positions and values, one can ask for a larger proportion of prescribed coefficients, an asymptotic count, or an efficient construction. The bounds above establish sufficient ranges; they need not be optimal or the strongest known for every pattern.

questions.title: Can degree and coefficient restrictions vary simultaneously?
questions.scope: A specified sequence of fields, degrees, and allowed coefficient sets
questions.body: The problem depends on which of \(q,n\) and the sets \(A_i\) vary. Cheng’s theorem allows increasing degree with large allowed sets, whereas the square-coefficient theorem fixes the degree. For a specified model, one can seek estimates uniform in both parameters or compare the ranges of these results. This formulation does not assert that every intermediate regime is open.
